The remarkable effectiveness of XGBoost was demonstrated in three distinct case studies: • Application 3 (disinfection): It proved to be the most accurate model for predicting both the required iCT and the resulting log removal of E. coli. • Application 4 (P-recovery): It delivered the best performance for predicting OP concentrations and, crucially, for classifying dosing conditions. • Application 5 (biosolids): It achieved the best predictive power for forecasting Total Solids percentages from the complex frequency data generated by acoustic sensors. 2.3.4 Support Vector Machines (SVM) A Support Vector Machine (SVM) operates on a different principle. It excels at finding the clearest possible boundary, or "hyperplane," that separates data points into different classes (Cortes and Vapnik 1995). By maximizing the margin, or distance, between the hyperplane and the nearest data points of each class (the "support vectors"), the SVM finds a robust decision boundary. A key advantage of SVMs is their effectiveness in high-dimensional spaces, where the number of features is very large relative to the number of samples. This characteristic made the SVM the most effective algorithm for the carbon diversion case study (Application 1). This problem was characterized by an exceptionally high-dimensional feature space, with over 120 12 The Water Research Foundation potential input variables influencing sludge settleability. The SVM was able to navigate this complexity to build the most successful predictive model. 2.3.5 The Time-Series Expert: Recurrent Neural Networks (LSTM) For challenges that involve data that unfold over time, a specialized class of models is required. Neural Networks, inspired by the interconnected structure of the human brain, are powerful function approximators capable of learning highly intricate patterns. Within this family, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are a type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) specifically architected to handle time-series data (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997). Unlike standard networks that treat each data point independently, LSTMs have internal loops and "memory cells" that allow them to retain information from previous time steps, enabling them to learn long-term dependencies in sequential data (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997). This unique capability made an LSTM-based model a critical component of the solution for BNR aeration control (Application 2). In this application, a hybrid model was developed that combined a mechanistic ASM1 model with a data-driven component. The data-driven part, an LSTM ensemble, was tasked with forecasting the error of the mechanistic model over time. By learning the temporal patterns in the mechanistic model's inaccuracies, the LSTM could provide a dynamic correction factor, significantly improving the overall predictive accuracy of the hybrid system and demonstrating a sophisticated application of LSTMs in wastewater treatment. The success of these different algorithms across the five case studies illustrates a deeper principle: algorithm selection is a form of hypothesis testing about the nature of the problem. Choosing an LSTM, as was done for Application 2, is an implicit hypothesis that temporal dependencies are the most critical pattern to capture.
